content: have/has been + doing shows an activity
that began earlier and still runs now.
"We have been renting this flat for two
years." — and we still rent it.
"She has been working since morning."
Started earlier, still going.
Form: have/has + been + the -ing form.
It ties the past start to this moment.
Many languages use a plain present here
("we rent it since two years"); English
reaches for have + been + doing.
for and since both measure the stretch
up to now — in different ways.
FOR + a length of time:
"It has been snowing for three days."
(how long: three days)
SINCE + a starting point:
"It has been snowing since Friday."
(from when: Friday onward)
for three hours / two years / a while.
since Friday / lunch / last week.
Many languages use one word for both;
English keeps for (length) and since
(start point) apart.
Modals can also GUESS from evidence,
not only give orders. This is
deduction.
SURE it is true — must be:
"Someone must be in the bedroom — the
light is on."
MAYBE — might / could / may be:
"She might be at home."
"It could be a mistake."
SURE it is NOT true — can't be:
"He can't be the thief; he was here
all night."
Warning: the 'no' of must here is
can't, NOT mustn't. 'Mustn't' forbids;
'can't be' means the evidence rules it
out.
Many languages weigh such a guess with
an adverb like 'surely' or 'maybe';
English bends its plain modals — must,
might, can't — to read the evidence.
